newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar seen rising despite US-Japan trade feud.
newsitem.headline: Dollar seen rising despite US-Japan trade feud.

text.p: The dollar is likely to challenge the crucial barrier of 125 yen within a month after a hike in U.S. interest rates on Tuesday, even though such a rise will increase trade friction between Tokyo and Washington.

The dollar got a boost on Wednesday after the U.S. Federal Reserve moved for the first time in more than two years to push its target for the key federal funds rate a quarter-point higher to 5.5 percent.
While the rate at which banks lend money to each other floats freely, the U.S. central bank can easily influence its level through money-market operations.

The risk for those betting on a dollar rise is that a stronger U.S. currency will make Japanese goods more competitive abroad and further anger Washington over Japan's huge trade surplus. The surplus with the United States totalled 407 billion yen ($3.28 billion) in February.

Richard Medley, president of Medley Investment Group and an advisor to the U.S. Democratic Party, told Reuters in an interview that the U.S. Treasury will not tolerate an increase in the structural trade deficit with Japan.
"The Treasury is growing concerned with the dollar at current levels, and above this level they will start to vocalise their concerns," he said.
Reflecting those worries, Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita acknowledged on Wednesday that the trade surplus is likely to rise but that it would be a gradual increase.
But trade friction worries are taking a back seat for now with Japanese investors buying dollars to invest fresh money overseas in the new fiscal year starting April 1, some traders said.
The dollar rose to 124.35 yen in late trading in Tokyo, its highest in more than a month and up from 123.30 on Tuesday before the Fed acted.

"I think that 125 yen will be perceived as a ceiling for now, but a steady flow of yen sales by Japanese could lift the dollar up to as high as around 127.50 yen within a month," said Ko Haruki, manager and chief dealer of forex sales at Midland Bank Plc.
Some analysts said that fundamental issues would also be pushing the dollar higher.

"It's a simple story. People are just buying dollars and selling the yen in light of the disparity in economic strength and interest rates between the United States and Japan," said Ichiro Ikeda, director of foreign exchange at Credit Suisse First Boston in Tokyo.
"The market rejoiced at the Fed's action because it would lead to a steady expansion in the U.S. economy without inflation. Meanwhile, the Japanese economy still looks fragile," he said.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said earlier this month that a dollar above 125 yen would cause trade friction with the United Sates, although in a sign of the sensitivity of the issue, he later withdrew the comment.
